If no BM for 5+ days despite maximal laxatives — consider clozapine dose reduction. Admission criteria: pain, distension, vomiting, no BM for 5+ days. Clozapine should never be stopped abruptly for constipation; it should be proactively managed. Clozapine-related mortality: aspiration pneumonia (most common) > myocarditis > bowel ischaemia > agranulocytosis.
source: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines; NICE CG178; Every-Palmer et al. (2017) Clozapine GI hypomotility

stem: A 31-year-old man with first-episode psychosis has been successfully treated with aripiprazole 15mg daily for 6 months and is now in remission. He has a BMI of 31 (gained 8kg over 6 months), HbA1c 42 mmol/mol, and his wife has expressed concern about his weight. What is the most appropriate management of his weight gain?
options: Switch to olanzapine which is weight neutral
Switch to paliperidone LAI which has less weight gain
Offer lifestyle advice (diet, exercise) and monitor weight, HbA1c and lipids; consider metformin or switching to lurasidone/ziprasidone if weight continues to increase
distractors_rationale: Olanzapine has MORE weight gain than aripiprazole (median ~4-5kg vs ~1-2kg). It would worsen the metabolic profile, not help.

Metformin is a useful treatment for antipsychotic-induced weight gain but should not be the first step. Lifestyle interventions and considering a switch should precede pharmacological management of weight gain.
Paliperidone has a similar weight gain profile to risperidone (moderate), which is more than aripiprazole. Switching from aripiprazole to paliperidone is likely to increase weight further.

CORRECT. NICE CG178 recommends: (1) Monitor weight, BMI, HbA1c, and lipids at baseline, 12 weeks, and annually; (2) Offer lifestyle advice (dietitian referral, exercise programme); (3) If weight gain continues despite lifestyle interventions, consider switching to an antipsychotic with lower metabolic risk (e.g., switching from aripiprazole — which is already low risk — would need to go to lurasidone or ziprasidone, which have the lowest metabolic impact but are less widely used). Metformin (off-label) can be considered if switching is not appropriate. Aripiprazole already has one of the best metabolic profiles, but 8kg gain in 6 months is significant and warrants active management.
Dose reduction may help but risks psychotic relapse. The weight gain on aripiprazole is partial D2 agonist mediated and not strictly dose-linear in terms of weight effect.
teaching_point: Weight gain hierarchy among antipsychotics (highest to lowest): Clozapine > Olanzapine > Risperidone / Paliperidone > Quetiapine > Amisulpride / Aripiprazole > Haloperidol > Lurasidone / Ziprasidone. Management of metabolic side effects: (1) Prevent with baseline monitoring and lifestyle counselling at initiation; (2) If >7% weight gain: switch to a lower-liability antipsychotic; (3) No switch possible: add metformin (off-label, 500-2000mg daily, ~3kg weight loss); (4) Consider orlistat (limited evidence in antipsychotic-induced obesity). NICE CG178: 'Do not routinely switch or stop antipsychotic to manage weight gain — offer lifestyle interventions first.' Aripiprazole is considered weight-neutral but some patients still gain significant weight.
source: NICE CG178; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines

stem: A 27-year-old woman with paranoid schizophrenia has a 5-year history although has not required hospitalisation. She has been stable on risperidone LAI 50mg IM every 2 weeks for the past 2 years. She has no history of cardiovascular disease and all baseline investigations were normal except for a mildly elevated prolactin of 750 mIU/L. She has noted galactorrhoea but no menstrual irregularities. She is asking about the possibility of pregnancy. She is currently using barrier contraception. What advice regarding medication in pregnancy should she be given?
options: She should stop risperidone before attempting pregnancy as it is teratogenic
The risks and benefits of continuing risperidone should be discussed; risperidone is relatively safe in pregnancy with neonatal adaptation monitored
Switch to olanzapine which is proven safe in pregnancy
Switch to clozapine before conception due to superior efficacy and safety
Increase barrier contraception and advise against pregnancy while on antipsychotics
distractors_rationale: Stopping all antipsychotics before pregnancy is dangerous — 70-80% of women with schizophrenia relapse in the first year off medication. Antipsychotics are not major teratogens (the absolute risk of major congenital malformations is increased by a small amount, approximately 2-3% vs 1-2% baseline).

CORRECT. NICE CG192 recommends: (1) Discuss risks of untreated psychosis in pregnancy (relapse, poor engagement, obstetric complications) vs small risks of antipsychotics; (2) Risperidone is considered relatively safe in pregnancy (extensive clinical experience, no specific major teratogenic pattern); (3) Monitor for gestational diabetes (antipsychotics increase risk); (4) Plan for neonatal adaptation syndrome (irritability, feeding difficulties, sedation — typically self-limiting, resolves within days); (5) Plan for the postnatal period (highest risk time).

Olanzapine is not 'proven safe' — no antipsychotic is proven safe (no RCTs in pregnancy). Olanzapine carries a higher risk of gestational diabetes and weight gain than risperidone. The choice should be based on what works best for the individual patient.

Clozapine requires stringent blood monitoring and is not recommended in pregnancy due to limited safety data and potential risk of agranulocytosis in the neonate. It is not a first-line choice in pregnancy.

Advising against pregnancy is ethically inappropriate. All patients have the right to make informed reproductive choices. The role of the psychiatrist is to counsel, support, and optimise treatment to allow the patient to have a safe pregnancy and healthy baby.
teaching_point: Antipsychotics in pregnancy: General principles: (1) Untreated maternal psychosis is harmful to both mother and baby (preterm birth, low birth weight, poor engagement); (2) Antipsychotics are not major teratogens — absolute risk of congenital anomalies is approximately 2-3% (vs 1-2% background); (3) High-potency FGAs (haloperidol) have the longest safety record; (4) Most SGAs (olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine) have moderate safety data; (5) Avoid polypharmacy where possible; (6) Monitor for gestational diabetes; (7) Plan for neonatal adaptation syndrome; (8) Arrange a perinatal psychiatry review. Risks per antipsychotic: olanzapine — highest gestational diabetes risk; risperidone — prolactin elevation may affect fertility; aripiprazole — limited data; clozapine — not first-line in pregnancy.
source: NICE CG192: Antenatal and postnatal mental health; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines

stem: A 34-year-old woman with schizophrenia (paranoid type) has been stable on paliperidone palmitate LAI 100mg IM monthly for 2 years. She wants to become pregnant and asks about the safest antipsychotic option. She has been in full remission for 18 months. What is the most appropriate recommendation?
options: Recommend switching to aripiprazole which has the best safety profile in pregnancy
Recommend continuing paliperidone as she is stable
Discuss the option of a planned off-medication trial before conception, with close monitoring
Recommend switching to haloperidol which has the longest safety record in pregnancy
Recommend switching to clozapine before conception
distractors_rationale: Aripiprazole has limited pregnancy safety data compared to haloperidol and FGAs. Switching carries risk of destabilisation.

Continuing paliperidone is an option, but the objective safest option (with the longest safety record) should be discussed. Paliperidone (active metabolite of risperidone) has similar safety data to risperidone.

CORRECT. Haloperidol (a high-potency FGA) has the longest safety record in pregnancy, with the most extensive published data dating back to the 1960s. It has not been associated with any specific major teratogenic pattern. The Maudsley Guidelines state: 'If a woman with schizophrenia is planning pregnancy, haloperidol is the antipsychotic of choice in terms of safety.' However, this must be balanced against the risk of destabilisation during a switch. Options for this patient: (1) Continue paliperidone (the devil you know — she is stable); (2) Switch to haloperidol or trifluoperazine (the safest safety record, higher EPS risk); (3) If she is in full remission and collaborative, a planned dose reduction with close perinatal team monitoring could be discussed. The choice should be individualised based on her history, resilience, and preferences. The patient should be seen in a specialist perinatal psychiatry service.
Haloperidol has the best evidence base. However, switching a stable patient carries relapse risk. Both approaches should be discussed.
Clozapine is not recommended in pregnancy and is not the safest option.
teaching_point: Antipsychotic choice in pregnancy — safety hierarchy (Maudsley, NICE CG192): Best evidence: Haloperidol, chlorpromazine, trifluoperazine (FGAs — extensive long-term data). Good evidence: Olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine (larger newer datasets). Limited evidence: Aripiprazole, paliperidone, amisulpride. Avoid if possible: Clozapine (requires strict blood monitoring, limited safety data), high-dose combinations. Key principle: A woman stable on an antipsychotic that is not known to be teratogenic should generally remain on it. Switching to haloperidol in pregnancy is only recommended if it provides a meaningful safety advantage without significant relapse risk. Most women remain on their current antipsychotic with appropriate monitoring.
source: NICE CG192; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines; BAP Guidelines (2017)

stem: A 30-year-old woman with a 10-year history of schizophrenia presents with a severe psychotic relapse. She has been non-adherent to oral antipsychotics in the past. She has previously tried risperidone (developed hyperprolactinaemia) and quetiapine (excessive sedation). She has a BMI of 34 with HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol (impaired fasting glucose). Her ECG shows QTc of 440ms. Which LAI antipsychotic is most appropriate?
distractors_rationale: Fluphenazine is a high-potency FGA with high EPS risk (parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia) and moderate prolactin elevation. It would be a poor choice given her previous hyperprolactinaemia on risperidone (FGAs can also cause this).

Olanzapine pamoate carries a risk of post-injection delirium/sedation syndrome (PDSS — 0.07% of injections), requires 3-hour post-injection observation, and has the highest metabolic risk (weight gain, diabetes) which is particularly dangerous given her BMI of 34 and impaired fasting glucose.

CORRECT. Aripiprazole LAI is an excellent choice because: (1) It does NOT cause hyperprolactinaemia (it can even lower prolactin — crucial given her risperidone history); (2) Low sedation profile (good given her quetiapine intolerance); (3) Weight NEUTRAL or minimal gain (safe with her obesity and borderline diabetes); (4) Minimal QTc prolongation; (5) Once-monthly dosing after initial loading (good for adherence); (6) Available as a long-acting injection. The LAI formulation addresses her adherence issues. The main side effect to monitor is akathisia (~10-15%).

Paliperidone palmitate has similar side effects to risperidone — hyperprolactinaemia and moderate weight gain. Given her history of hyperprolactinaemia on risperidone, paliperidone (its active metabolite) is likely to cause the same issue.
Haloperidol decanoate carries high EPS risk, moderate QTc prolongation risk, hyperprolactinaemia, and postural hypotension. It is a poor choice given her risk factors.
teaching_point: LAI antipsychotic selection — individualised choice based on side-effect history: Aripiprazole LAI is unique among LAIs: (1) Weight neutral (critical in patients with metabolic risk); (2) No prolactin elevation; (3) Minimal QTc effect; (4) Low sedation; (5) Once-monthly (paliperidone also has 3-monthly). The patient's history of hyperprolactinaemia on risperidone is the key discriminating factor. Aripiprazole (partial D2 agonist) is prolactin-sparing — it can even treat risperidone-induced hyperprolactinaemia. Side-effect profile is the main determinant of LAI choice — not just efficacy.
source: NICE CG178; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines

stem: A 50-year-old man with chronic schizophrenia who is a heavy smoker (40/day) has been on olanzapine 10mg daily with poor response. On assessment, his smoking has increased recently. His baseline olanzapine level is subtherapeutic. Smoking cessation is planned. What is the most important consideration when he stops smoking?
options: Olanzapine levels may decrease — increase the dose
Olanzapine levels may increase due to CYP1A2 de-induction — halve or reduce the dose and monitor for toxicity
No dose change needed — smoking does not affect olanzapine
Switch to aripiprazole which is not CYP1A2-metabolised
Add nicotine replacement therapy to maintain olanzapine levels
distractors_rationale: Olanzapine levels INCREASE when smoking stops (smoking induces CYP1A2). They do not decrease.

CORRECT. Smoking induces CYP1A2 (the major enzyme that metabolises clozapine and olanzapine). When a heavy smoker stops smoking, CYP1A2 activity decreases over 2-4 weeks, leading to a significant INCREASE in olanzapine levels (by up to 50-100%). This can cause toxicity (excessive sedation, hypotension, seizures). Management: (1) Warn the patient; (2) Consider reducing the olanzapine dose by 30-50% at the time of smoking cessation; (3) Monitor for side effects; (4) Recheck levels in 2-4 weeks. The same principle applies to clozapine — it is the most important drug interaction in clozapine prescribing.
Smoking DOES affect olanzapine — it's a key exam fact. CYP1A2 is induced by polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in cigarette smoke.
Aripiprazole is metabolised by CYP2D6 and CYP3A4, not CYP1A2, so smoking does not affect its levels. This is an option but the immediate safety concern is the olanzapine level change.

Nicotine replacement (patches, gum) does NOT induce CYP1A2 — only the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in SMOKE do. So nicotine replacement alone does not alter olanzapine/clozapine metabolism. However, it does not address the dose adjustment need.
teaching_point: Smoking and antipsychotics — the CYP1A2 interaction: This is one of the most important drug interactions in psychiatry. Cigarette smoke (specifically polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons) induces CYP1A2, increasing the metabolism of clozapine and olanzapine by up to 40-50%. A heavy smoker may need up to double the dose of a non-smoker. When a patient stops smoking (or is admitted to a smoke-free ward), CYP1A2 de-induction over 2-4 weeks causes levels to RISE by up to 50-100%, risking toxicity. Management: reduce clozapine/olanzapine dose by 30-50% when smoking cessation is planned. Monitor levels. Other CYP1A2 inducers: char-grilled meat, cruciferous vegetables (broccoli, Brussels sprouts). Inhibitors: fluvoxamine, caffeine (weak), grapefruit juice. Aripiprazole, risperidone, quetiapine, and haloperidol are NOT metabolised by CYP1A2 and are not affected by smoking.
source: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines; NICE CG178; BNF

stem: A 44-year-old man with schizophrenia on clozapine 400mg daily is admitted to a smoke-free ward. He smokes 30 cigarettes per day. Three days after admission, he becomes excessively sedated, drooling, and ataxic. What is the most likely cause of this presentation?
options: Clozapine toxicity due to smoking cessation-induced CYP1A2 de-induction
distractors_rationale: Myocarditis presents with fever, chest pain, dyspnoea, and elevated troponin — not excessive sedation, drooling, and ataxia without fever.
NMS presents with fever, rigidity, autonomic instability, and elevated CK — not excessive sedation and drooling without rigidity or fever.

CORRECT. This is a classic and important clinical scenario. Smoking cessation causes CYP1A2 de-induction over 1-4 weeks. Since clozapine is predominantly metabolised by CYP1A2, cessation of smoking in a heavy smoker can double serum clozapine levels, leading to acute toxicity. Symptoms of clozapine toxicity: excessive sedation, drooling/hypersalivation, ataxia, confusion, seizures (at high levels). Management: (1) Hold the next dose; (2) Check clozapine level urgently; (3) Reduce dose by 30-50% and monitor symptoms; (4) If severe (seizures, respiratory depression), admit to medical ward. The same applies to olanzapine. Prevention: reduce clozapine/olanzapine dose by 30-50% at the time of admission to a smoke-free ward.

A CVA would present with focal neurological signs (hemiparesis, facial droop, dysphasia), not with the global picture of sedation and ataxia without focal features in a patient with a clear alternative explanation.
Benzodiazepine withdrawal presents with anxiety, agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, and seizures — not excessive sedation and drooling.
teaching_point: Clozapine toxicity from smoking cessation — classic MRCPsych exam scenario: Mechanism: smoking induces CYP1A2 → smoking stops → CYP1A2 de-induction over 1-2 weeks → clozapine levels rise 50-100%. Clinical features of toxicity: sedation (most sensitive indicator), hypersalivation, ataxia, confusion, seizures (levels >1000-1300 ng/mL), respiratory depression, coma. Management: stop clozapine, check level, supportive care, reduce dose. Prevention: anticipate at admission — reduce dose by 30-50% when a smoker is admitted to a smoke-free setting. Monitor levels weekly during the transition. The same interaction applies to olanzapine but is less dramatic. CYP1A2 is also induced by: cannabis smoking, chargrilled meat, cruciferous vegetables. Inhibited by: fluvoxamine (potent), ciprofloxacin, caffeine (mild).
source: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines; BNF; NICE CG178

stem: According to research evidence, which of the following is most strongly associated with first-episode psychosis coming to clinical attention earlier (shorter duration of untreated psychosis)?
options: The patient being from an ethnic minority background
The presence of family involvement and help-seeking
The type of psychotic symptoms (positive vs negative)
distractors_rationale: Ethnic minority status is associated with LONGER DUP and later presentation to EIP services, not shorter.
Higher premorbid functioning is associated with better outcomes but has a complex relationship with DUP (may be associated with later presentation as the patient may compensate better initially).

CORRECT. Family involvement and active help-seeking by family members is the strongest factor associated with shorter DUP. The family may notice symptoms earlier, be more motivated to seek help, and engage more effectively with healthcare services. Other factors associated with shorter DUP: (1) acute onset (vs insidious); (2) living in urban areas with better access to EIP services; (3) younger age at onset; (4) presence of violent or risky behaviour. Longer DUP is associated with: insidious onset, negative symptoms, male gender, ethnic minority status, living alone, lower socio-economic status.

The type of psychotic symptoms (e.g., positive vs negative) has a complex relationship with DUP. Predominantly negative symptoms are associated with LONGER DUP (they are less noticeable and more likely to be attributed to adolescent turmoil or personality). Positive symptoms (especially if behavioural) may lead to earlier presentation.
Male gender is associated with LONGER DUP in some studies (though the evidence is mixed).
teaching_point: Duration of Untreated Psychosis (DUP): Mean DUP is 1-2 years in UK (varies widely from weeks to years). Shorter DUP → better outcomes (treatment response, symptom remission, social functioning, cognition). Factors associated with shorter DUP: family involvement, acute onset, younger age, living with family. Factors associated with longer DUP: insidious onset, negative symptoms, ethnic minority, male, living alone, poor premorbid functioning. EIP services aim to reduce DUP. The 2-week wait target (NHS Long Term Plan) is designed to minimise DUP. Critical/sensitive period hypothesis: the first 2-5 years after onset are a critical period where intervention can fundamentally alter illness trajectory.
source: Marshall M et al. (2005) DUP and outcome: systematic review. Br J Psychiatry; NICE CG178

stem: A 46-year-old man with chronic schizophrenia is being reviewed by the assertive outreach team at home. He has had multiple hospital admissions over the past 10 years due to poor adherence with oral medication. He has previously tried olanzapine (weight gain of 12kg), risperidone (prolactin-related sexual dysfunction), and haloperidol (severe akathisia). He is currently not on any medication and is moderately symptomatic with paranoid ideas and social withdrawal. He agrees to consider a depot/LAI. What is the most appropriate LAI to offer?
distractors_rationale: CORRECT. Paliperidone palmitate (a monthly LAI) is a good choice here. Paliperidone is the active 9-hydroxy metabolite of risperidone. It has a distinct side-effect profile — while it shares prolactin elevation (which may be a problem given his history of risperidone-related sexual dysfunction), it has: less sedation than olanzapine, less weight gain than olanzapine, less akathisia than haloperidol, and less EPS than FGAs. The monthly dosing schedule (after initial loading days 1 and 8) is simpler for adherence. However, note the prolactin issue — in practice aripiprazole LAI would be preferred given his side-effect history, but it's not listed here. Between the options, paliperidone is the most appropriate.

Olanzapine pamoate (LAI) requires 3-hour post-injection monitoring for PDSS. Given his history of significant weight gain on oral olanzapine, this LAI would likely cause further metabolic deterioration.
Zuclopenthixol is a high-potency FGA depot, carries EPS risk and akathisia. Given his history of akathisia on haloperidol (also a high-potency FGA), this should be avoided.
Haloperidol decanoate has the same problems — high akathisia risk. His history clearly contraindicates this.

Flupentixol decanoate is a moderate-potency FGA depot — lower akathisia risk than haloperidol but still significant EPS risk. However, given his poor experience with haloperidol (akathisia), FGAs should be avoided.
teaching_point: Selecting an LAI after multiple antipsychotic failures: The key is to review side-effect history and select a drug with a different profile. This patient had EPS with haloperidol (FGA) and weight gain with olanzapine (SGA with high metabolic risk). The remaining options are: (1) Paliperidone (moderate side-effect profile, prolactin risk); (2) Aripiprazole (best profile for this patient — would be ideal but wasn't listed). The principle: choose an LAI based on the patient's response and tolerance history. If a patient has failed multiple antipsychotics, consider a different mechanism (e.g., a partial agonist like aripiprazole). Paliperidone LAI evidence: similar efficacy to risperidone LAI but monthly dosing is preferred by patients. The loading regimen: 150mg IM day 1, 100mg IM day 8, then 75-150mg monthly.
source: NICE CG178; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines

stem: A 39-year-old man with schizophrenia who has been well on quetiapine 400mg daily for 3 years presents at a routine review. His psychotic symptoms remain well controlled but he reports being unable to achieve or maintain an erection, which is causing significant distress and relationship problems. His prolactin level is normal. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Reassure that this is a common side effect that usually resolves
distractors_rationale: Aripiprazole has a lower rate of sexual dysfunction than quetiapine but switching carries relapse risk and may not be necessary if the sexual dysfunction can be managed more simply. The patient is stable on quetiapine.

CORRECT. Quetiapine can cause sexual dysfunction via dopamine blockade (D2) in the tuberoinfundibular pathway, histamine blockade (sedation affecting libido and performance), and alpha-1 blockade (affecting erection). The most common management for antipsychotic-induced erectile dysfunction is: (1) Check prolactin (if high → switch to a prolactin-sparing agent); (2) If prolactin normal and the patient wishes to continue the current antipsychotic, consider a PDE5 inhibitor (sildenafil, tadalafil). Sildenafil 50mg is effective for antipsychotic-induced erectile dysfunction. Alternatives: dose reduction (risks relapse), switch to aripiprazole (if acceptable to the patient).
Testosterone is not routinely recommended without confirmed biochemical hypogonadism. It carries risks (prostate, cardiovascular) and is not first-line.
Dose reduction may help but risks psychotic relapse. Sexual dysfunction with quetiapine can occur even at moderate doses.
Reassurance is insufficient. The patient is distressed and the problem is causing relationship difficulties. Active management is needed.
teaching_point: Antipsychotic-induced sexual dysfunction: Mechanisms vary: (1) Prolactin elevation (risperidone, amisulpride, haloperidol) → decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, anorgasmia; (2) Dopamine antagonism (all antipsychotics to varying degrees) → decreased libido; (3) Alpha-1 blockade (quetiapine, chlorpromazine) → erectile dysfunction; (4) Histamine H1 blockade → sedation affecting sexual function. Management: (1) Check prolactin; (2) If raised → switch to prolactin-sparing agent (aripiprazole, quetiapine, olanzapine); (3) If prolactin normal → consider PDE5 inhibitor (sildenafil) for erectile dysfunction; (4) Consider dose reduction (risks relapse); (5) Consider switch to aripiprazole. Aripiprazole has the lowest rate of sexual dysfunction among antipsychotics. Sexual dysfunction affects 30-70% of patients on antipsychotics and is a major cause of non-adherence.
source: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines; Montejo AL et al. (2018) Antipsychotic-related sexual dysfunction

stem: A 33-year-old man with first-episode psychosis has been on aripiprazole 10mg daily for 8 weeks with good resolution of positive symptoms. However, he reports persistent lack of motivation (avolition), social withdrawal, and reduced emotional expression. These symptoms were present before treatment but have become more noticeable now that his positive symptoms have resolved. He has no depressive symptoms, no EPS, and his aripiprazole dose is within the normal range. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Increase aripiprazole to 15mg daily to better treat the negative symptoms
Diagnose post-psychotic depression and start an SSRI
Add cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis (CBTp) and consider a trial of switching or augmenting with a drug that may improve negative symptoms
Add an anticholinergic (procyclidine) to rule out drug-induced akinesia
Reassure that these symptoms are part of the illness and cannot be treated
distractors_rationale: Increasing aripiprazole is unlikely to help and may worsen negative symptoms (D2 blockade causing secondary negative symptoms).
Post-psychotic depression requires depressive symptoms (low mood, anhedonia, worthlessness) beyond negative symptoms. This patient has negative symptoms without depressive cognitions.

CORRECT. Primary negative symptoms persisting after resolution of positive symptoms are a therapeutic challenge. Management: (1) Rule out secondary causes (depression, EPS, medication-induced akinesia, social deprivation); (2) Offer CBTp specifically adapted for negative symptoms (evidence for small to moderate improvement in avolition and social functioning); (3) Consider switching to amisulpride (has the best evidence for primary negative symptoms at low doses 50-300mg via presynaptic D2/D3 blockade enhancing prefrontal dopamine); (4) Consider aripiprazole augmentation with low-dose amisulpride; (5) Consider psychosocial interventions (social skills training, supported employment). Clozapine may improve secondary negative symptoms but evidence for primary negative symptoms is mixed.
Anticholinergics would only help if there is drug-induced akinesia (which mimics negative symptoms). This patient has no EPS, making this unlikely.
This is an outdated and incorrect view. Negative symptoms are challenging but not untreatable.
teaching_point: Primary vs secondary negative symptoms — the key distinction for MRCPsych: SECONDARY negative symptoms (treatable causes): (1) Positive symptoms (social withdrawal due to paranoia); (2) Depression; (3) EPS (akinesia, bradykinesia); (4) Sedation from medication; (5) Environmental deprivation. PRIMARY negative symptoms (deficit syndrome): core illness features with no identifiable secondary cause. Treatment of primary negative symptoms: (1) CBT (best evidence); (2) Amisulpride (low dose, evidence from Cochrane review, Leucht et al. 2013); (3) Aripiprazole augmentation; (4) Psychosocial interventions; (5) No strong evidence for SSRIs, modafinil, or other agents. Amisulpride's unique mechanism: at low doses (<300mg), preferentially blocks presynaptic D2/D3 autoreceptors, increasing dopamine release in the prefrontal cortex.
source: NICE CG178; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines; Leucht S et al. (2013) Amisulpride for negative symptoms

stem: Which one of the following antipsychotics carries the HIGHEST risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE)?
distractors_rationale: Aripiprazole has the lowest VTE risk due to its neutral metabolic and platelet effects.
Risperidone has intermediate VTE risk, higher than aripiprazole but lower than clozapine.

CORRECT. Clozapine carries the highest VTE risk of all antipsychotics (odds ratio ~2.5-6.5). The mechanism is multifactorial: (1) Sedation and immobility; (2) Obesity; (3) Increased platelet aggregation; (4) Elevated anticardiolipin antibodies (some patients); (5) Hyperhomocysteinaemia. VTE risk is highest in the first 3-6 months of treatment. Clozapine-associated VTE is frequently under-recognised. Any patient on clozapine presenting with unilateral leg swelling, chest pain, or sudden dyspnoea should be investigated for DVT/PE. Antipsychotics as a class increase VTE risk by 2-3× (population-based studies). Low-potency FGAs (chlorpromazine) and clozapine have the highest risk. Prophylactic measures: hydration, mobilisation, compression stockings, and VTE risk assessment.
Haloperidol has a lower VTE risk than low-potency antipsychotics. High-potency FGAs have less VTE risk than low-potency ones.
Quetiapine has moderate VTE risk (similar to olanzapine and risperidone), lower than clozapine.
teaching_point: Antipsychotics and VTE: A meta-analysis of observational studies (Zhang et al., 2021) found: all antipsychotics increase VTE risk (OR ~2.0). Risk hierarchy: Clozapine (highest) > Low-potency FGAs (chlorpromazine) > Olanzapine/Quetiapine/Risperidone > Haloperidol/Aripiprazole (lowest). VTE is one of the most under-recognised antipsychotic-related adverse events. Clinical presentation: unilateral calf swelling/Homans sign (DVT), sudden dyspnoea/tachypnoea/pleuritic chest pain/ haemoptysis (PE). Risk factors for VTE: age >60, obesity, smoking, immobility, surgery, travel, pregnancy, oestrogen therapy, cancer, thrombophilia. Monitoring: ask about leg swelling/chest pain at each clozapine review. Prevention for clozapine: maintain hydration, encourage mobilisation, weight management.
source: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines; Zhang R et al. (2021) Antipsychotics and VTE; BNF

stem: A 47-year-old woman with a 25-year history of schizophrenia is brought to the emergency department by police after being found wandering the streets in a confused and agitated state. She is well-known to the mental health team and had disengaged from services 3 months ago. Her last prescribed medication was flupentixol decanoate 40mg IM every 2 weeks. She is poor historian, appears frightened, and is responding to unseen stimuli. Observations: BP 145/90, HR 102, Temp 37.1°C, RR 18, O2 sat 99%. Blood glucose 7.2 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Administer haloperidol 5mg IM for rapid tranquillisation
Start olanzapine 10mg orally as a stat dose and restart depot in the morning
Reassure and observe in a quiet room overnight
Initiate clozapine 12.5mg BD for suspected treatment resistance
distractors_rationale: Haloperidol is not indicated here. The patient has baseline tachycardia and hypertension — haloperidol carries dystonia and QTc risks. There is no acute risk justifying pharmacological sedation.
Oral olanzapine stat is premature — she may be distressed but not acutely aggressive or at risk. A less invasive approach should be tried first.

CORRECT. This patient is likely experiencing a psychotic relapse due to disengagement and missed depot medications. She is frightened and confused but has normal observations (no acute medical issue), normal glucose (stress hyperglycaemia likely), and is not aggressive. The appropriate initial management is: (1) Place in a quiet, low-stimulation environment; (2) Provide reassurance and reorientation; (3) Re-establish oral intake and hydration; (4) Contact the home treatment team or EIP service; (5) Consider oral antipsychotic (the same medication she was on) if she is unable to settle; (6) Restart her depot once she is medically stable and consent is obtained. This is a common presentation of disengagement. The principle: least restrictive first.
Restarting a depot requires capacity assessment and consent. In a confused/frightened patient, this may not be appropriate without first assessing capacity and attempting oral medication.
There is no evidence of treatment resistance. Clozapine would be inappropriate — it requires FBC monitoring, slow titration, and is indicated after 2 failed antipsychotic trials at adequate doses.
teaching_point: Management of relapsed psychosis after disengagement from services: Prevalence: up to 50% of patients with schizophrenia disengage from services at some point. Approach: (1) Assess capacity to consent to treatment; (2) If the patient lacks capacity, treat under MCA (best interests) or MHA; (3) Offer oral antipsychotic (same as previous effective agent); (4) Re-engage with community team, home treatment, or EIP; (5) Re-establish depot/LAI if previously effective; (6) Assess for physical health complications of relapse (dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, VTE risk). Least restrictive principle: always start with the least coercive intervention. The MHA may be needed if the patient lacks capacity and needs treatment for a mental disorder that places themselves or others at risk.
source: NICE CG178; MHA 1983 Code of Practice; MCA 2005

stem: A 55-year-old man with a 30-year history of schizophrenia has been maintained on flupentixol decanoate (depot) 40mg IM every 2 weeks with good effect. He develops choreiform movements of his mouth and tongue. What is the most appropriate management step?
options: Reduce depot frequency to every 3 weeks
Increase depot dose to suppress the movements
distractors_rationale: Procyclidine (anticholinergic) can WORSEN tardive dyskinesia (TD). Anticholinergics reduce the threshold for TD and should be tapered if possible. They may help acute dystonia and parkinsonism but NOT TD.
Reducing the dose may help by lowering D2 blockade but carries risk of psychotic relapse. Switching to a lower TD-risk antipsychotic (clozapine or aripiprazole) is the recommended approach.

CORRECT. The first-line management of tardive dyskinesia is: (1) Switch to clozapine (best evidence for TD improvement) OR aripiprazole (partial D2 agonist, evidence for TD improvement). (2) Reduce or stop anticholinergic medications. (3) If the movements are severe and disabling, consider VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine — not widely available in UK NHS, or tetrabenazine off-label). (4) Consider adding vitamin E (limited evidence). Aripiprazole LAI is a practical option: ensures adherence, months-monthly dosing, and has a lower TD risk than flupentixol (FGA). Clozapine would be first-line if the patient has treatment-resistant symptoms.

Tetrabenazine is a VMAT2 inhibitor used for Huntington's chorea. It carries risk of depression and parkinsonism. It is not first-line for antipsychotic-induced TD and should only be considered under specialist advice.

Increasing the depot dose would mask TD temporarily but worsen the underlying D2 supersensitivity. When the dose is eventually reduced, the movements would worsen (withdrawal-emergent TD). This is never recommended.
teaching_point: Tardive dyskinesia — management summary: Step 1: Switch to clozapine (first-line, evidence from multiple studies — improvement in 50-60%) or aripiprazole (partial agonist). Step 2: Taper and stop anticholinergics. Step 3: Consider VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine, tetrabenazine) under specialist guidance. Step 4: Consider vitamin E (weak evidence). TD develops in 20-30% of long-term FGA users. FGAs (haloperidol, fluphenazine, flupentxol, zuclopenthixol) carry the highest risk. SGAs (olanzapine, risperidone) carry moderate risk. Clozapine, quetiapine, and aripiprazole carry the lowest risk. AIMS (Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale) is the standard monitoring tool. Withdrawal-emergent TD: can occur when antipsychotic is reduced or stopped — do not restart the antipsychotic to mask it.
source: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines; NICE CG178; Bhidayasiri R et al. (2018) TD management

stem: A 26-year-old man presents with his first episode of psychosis — he has persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations that have been present for about 6 weeks with a 4-month prodromal phase of social withdrawal and declining function. He has no medical history, no substance use, and baseline investigations are normal. He agrees to start antipsychotic medication. According to NICE, what is the recommended timeframe for assessing response to an antipsychotic trial?
options: 4-6 weeks at an adequate therapeutic dose
8-12 weeks at an adequate therapeutic dose
distractors_rationale: 2 weeks is insufficient to assess response. Some early improvement may be seen, but full assessment requires 4-6 weeks.

CORRECT. NICE CG178 states: 'Assess response to antipsychotic medication after 4-6 weeks at an adequate therapeutic dose. If there is no improvement after 4-6 weeks, consider switching to a different antipsychotic.' If there is some response but suboptimal, the trial can be extended to 8-12 weeks. The dose should be within the therapeutic range (BNF-listed dose), not a subtherapeutic dose. Response is defined as: (1) >20% reduction in PANSS/BPRS; (2) CGI-I of much/very much improved; (3) Improvement in social/occupational functioning.
8-12 weeks is too long to wait without response and risks prolonged untreated symptoms. Only extend to 8-12 weeks if there is partial response.
3 months is too long and the dose must be adequate.
1 week is far too short, and subtherapeutic doses cannot be adequately assessed.
teaching_point: Timing of antipsychotic response: Early improvement (weeks 1-2) predicts eventual response, but the formal assessment is at 4-6 weeks. If there is no improvement at 4-6 weeks, switch to a different antipsychotic (different class ideally). After two adequate trials at 4-6 weeks each, assess for treatment resistance and consider clozapine. The Maudsley guidelines note that some patients (especially on clozapine/olanzapine) may show slower improvement up to 12 weeks. Key exam point: treatment resistance is defined as failure of at least TWO antipsychotic trials of adequate dose and duration (6 weeks each).
source: NICE CG178; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines

stem: A 36-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been on clozapine 500mg daily for 3 months. His positive symptoms have improved but he continues to experience significant persistent auditory hallucinations and paranoid beliefs. His clozapine level is 550 ng/mL. Adherence is confirmed. He has had trials of risperidone and olanzapine previously. Which of the following augmentation strategies has the strongest evidence base?
distractors_rationale: Lamotrigine augmentation has mixed evidence. Some positive open-label trials but RCTs have been inconclusive. It also carries Stevens-Johnson syndrome risk with slow titration required.
Valproate augmentation has been studied, but evidence is weak. It is not recommended by NICE or Maudsley for clozapine augmentation.

CORRECT. Amisulpride augmentation has the strongest evidence base for clozapine non-response among antipsychotic augmentation strategies. A meta-analysis by Taylor et al. (2012) and subsequent studies found: adding amisulpride (400-800mg daily) to clozapine produces significant improvement in positive and negative symptoms. The mechanism: amisulpride's high D2/D3 occupancy complements clozapine's broad receptor profile and low D2 occupancy. Other augmentation strategies with evidence: aripiprazole (moderate evidence, also helps weight), and ECT (strong evidence but reserved for severe cases).

ECT has strong evidence for augmentation in clozapine-resistant schizophrenia (response rate 40-60%), but it is not first-line augmentation. It is reserved for severe symptoms, catatonia, or high suicide risk.

Aripiprazole augmentation has moderate evidence (some positive RCTs). It may help weight gain as an added benefit. However, amisulpride has the strongest evidence base for positive symptom improvement.
teaching_point: Clozapine augmentation strategies — evidence hierarchy: (1) Amisulpride (best evidence, D2/D3 antagonist); (2) Aripiprazole (moderate evidence, partial D2 agonist, helps weight); (3) ECT (strong evidence but invasive, reserved for severe/resistant); (4) Lamotrigine (weak evidence, SJS risk); (5) Sulpiride (similar to amisulpride, less studied); (6) Valproate (no convincing evidence); (7) The Maudsley Guidelines also mention: pimozide, haloperidol, chlorpromazine augmentation but with lower evidence. The most common practice: amisulpride 400-800mg daily added to clozapine. Monitor for QTc, check U&Es/BNF. About 30-50% of patients who have not responded to clozapine monotherapy will respond to augmentation.
source: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines; Taylor DM et al. (2012) Clozapine augmentation; NICE CG178

stem: A 32-year-old woman with a 14-year history of schizophrenia is being assessed in a pre-conception counselling appointment. She has been stable on aripiprazole LAI 400mg monthly for 2 years. She has had two previous episodes of severe postpartum psychosis requiring admission to a mother and baby unit. She wishes to understand the risks and benefits of continuing medication in pregnancy. According to NICE, what is the most appropriate advice?
options: Aripiprazole should be discontinued before conception as it has known teratogenic effects
The benefits of continuing aripiprazole likely outweigh the small risks (unknown risk profile but no major teratogenic signal); discuss the plan with specialist perinatal services
Switch to haloperidol as it is the only antipsychotic proven safe in pregnancy
Recommend termination of pregnancy if she conceives on aripiprazole
Recommend she discontinue all medication and rely on psychological therapy alone
distractors_rationale: Aripiprazole is not known to be a major teratogen. No specific pattern of congenital malformations has been identified, though data are less extensive than for older antipsychotics.

CORRECT. NICE CG192 recommends: (1) Discuss the risks of untreated mental illness in pregnancy (relapse, disengagement, poor obstetric outcomes) vs the risks of medication; (2) Aripiprazole is not a known major teratogen but data are limited — the woman should be counselled about the limited evidence base; (3) The lowest effective dose should be used; (4) She should have a detailed discussion with a specialist perinatal psychiatrist; (5) If she conceives while on aripiprazole, she should be supported to continue (if that is her preference) with close monitoring; (6) There is no evidence to recommend switching to haloperidol in a woman stable on aripiprazole.

Haloperidol has the most extensive safety database in pregnancy, but switching a stable patient carries relapse risk. The principle of 'don't fix what isn't broken' applies. Haloperidol would only be recommended if the patient chooses to switch after understanding the risks.
Termination is not recommended based solely on antipsychotic exposure. The overall risk of major congenital malformations with most antipsychotics is approximately 2-3% (baseline 1-2%).
Discontinuing all medication is dangerous given her history of severe postpartum psychosis (high relapse risk without medication).
teaching_point: Antipsychotics in pregnancy — NICE CG192 key principles: (1) Untreated maternal mental illness carries significant risks (relapse, poor obstetric outcomes, impaired mother-infant bonding, safeguarding concerns). (2) Most antipsychotics are not major teratogens. (3) The risk of relapse after stopping antipsychotics in pregnancy is high (50-70% for schizophrenia). (4) If a woman is stable on an antipsychotic and there is no known teratogenicity, it is generally recommended to continue. (5) Switch only if there is a specific safety concern outweighing the risk of destabilisation. (6) Refer all women with severe mental illness in pregnancy to specialist perinatal services. (7) Plan for the postnatal period (highest risk time for relapse). Aripiprazole safety data: limited but growing; no specific teratogenic pattern identified.
source: NICE CG192: Antenatal and postnatal mental health; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines

stem: A 50-year-old man with chronic schizophrenia has been stable on flupentixol decanoate 40mg IM every 2 weeks for 5 years. He is found to have a corrected QT interval (QTc) of 485ms on a routine ECG. His electrolytes are normal. He has no history of cardiac disease and is on no other QTc-prolonging medications. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Continue flupentixol and repeat ECG in 6 months
Switch to haloperidol decanoate as it has less QTc effect
Add amiodarone 200mg daily for QT prophylaxis
Switch to aripiprazole LAI (which has minimal QTc effect) and refer to cardiology
distractors_rationale: A QTc of 485ms is prolonged (>470ms in men is abnormal) and requires action. Active management is needed, not just monitoring.
Haloperidol also prolongs QTc (dose-dependent) and carries additional EPS and metabolic risks. It is not a safer alternative.

Amiodarone itself is a QTc-prolonging antiarrhythmic with significant side effects (thyroid, pulmonary, hepatic). It is NEVER used for drug-induced QTc prolongation. Management of prolonged QTc is to remove the offending drug.

CORRECT. A QTc >480ms in a patient on a QTc-prolonging antipsychotic requires: (1) Stop the offending drug; (2) Correct electrolyte abnormalities; (3) ECG monitoring; (4) Refer to cardiology if QTc does not normalise; (5) Switch to a lower-risk antipsychotic (aripiprazole has minimal QTc effect, as does lurasidone and ziprasidone — though the latter are not widely available in the UK). Aripiprazole LAI is an appropriate switch option. Maudsley Guidelines: consider switch to aripiprazole if QTc is >480ms on a QTc-prolonging antipsychotic.
Dose reduction may help marginally but does not address the underlying issue. Flupentixol still has significant QTc prolongation even at lower doses. Switching is preferred.
teaching_point: QTc prolongation management on antipsychotics: Thresholds: Normal QTc <440ms (men) / <460ms (women). Borderline 440-470ms (men) / 460-480ms (women). Prolonged >470ms (men) / >480ms (women). If QTc >500ms or increased by >60ms from baseline: immediate action. Management steps: (1) Check electrolytes (K+, Mg2+, Ca2+); (2) Review all QTc-prolonging drugs (antipsychotics, antibiotics, antiemetics); (3) Stop the offending drug; (4) Switch to a QTc-neutral antipsychotic (aripiprazole, lurasidone); (5) Cardiology referral if QTc remains prolonged; (6) Avoid other QTc-prolonging drugs in future. Antipsychotic QTc risk: Haloperidol (IV > oral, dose-dependent) > Amisulpride (dose-dependent) > Quetiapine > Risperidone > Olanzapine > Aripiprazole (lowest).
source: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines; BNF; NICE CG178

stem: A 38-year-old woman with paranoid schizophrenia develops severe NMS while on haloperidol 15mg daily. She has marked rigidity, fever (39.2°C), autonomic instability, and a CK of 25,000 IU/L. Haloperidol has been stopped and IV fluids started. What is the most appropriate specific pharmacological treatment for her NMS?
distractors_rationale: Procyclidine (anticholinergic) is for acute dystonia and parkinsonism — not NMS. It does not treat the core pathophysiology of NMS.
L-dopa is used for Parkinson's disease. It increases CNS dopamine but carries psychosis risk. It is not standard treatment for NMS.
ECT is effective for NMS (especially for catatonic features and refractory cases) but is a SECOND-LINE treatment after pharmacological measures and supportive care have been tried.

CORRECT. Moderate-severe NMS (CK >10,000, marked rigidity, fever, autonomic instability) requires specific pharmacological treatment in addition to supportive care (stop antipsychotic, IV fluids, cooling). First-line: dantrolene (direct-acting skeletal muscle relaxant, reduces rigidity and heat production) 50-100mg IV, or bromocriptine (dopamine agonist, addresses dopamine blockade) 5-10mg TDS. Dantrolene works faster on rigidity; bromocriptine addresses neuropsychiatric symptoms and may prevent recurrence. The two can be combined if there is no response. Supportive care includes: IV fluids (for rhabdomyolysis), cooling, anticoagulation (VTE risk), and monitoring for complications (AKI, DIC, ARDS, aspiration).

Midazolam is for sedation and may be used for acute agitation but does not treat NMS. Benzodiazepines alone (lorazepam 1-2mg) are used for malignant catatonia, which can be hard to distinguish from NMS.
teaching_point: NMS management: The three pillars — (1) SUPPORTIVE: stop antipsychotic, IV fluids (for rhabdomyolysis-induced AKI), cooling (for hyperthermia), monitoring (CK, U&Es, urine output, VTE prophylaxis). (2) SPECIFIC: dantrolene (2-3mg/kg/day IV — reduces rigidity, heat production), bromocriptine (5-10mg TDS — dopamine agonist), or both. (3) ECT: if refractory or severe (especially if catatonic features). NMS typically resolves over 5-14 days but CK may take longer. Recovery rate: 80-90% with modern management. Mortality: 5-10% (down from 20-30% historically). After recovery, reintroduce antipsychotics cautiously (wait 2 weeks, use a low-potency agent). Clozapine and quetiapine have the lowest NMS risk. Do NOT rechallenge with the offending drug.
source: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines; Strawn JR et al. (2007) NMS; BNF

stem: A 33-year-old man with schizophrenia has been stable on risperidone LAI 50mg IM every 2 weeks for the past year. He comes to clinic complaining that he has been feeling 'not quite right' for the past week — slightly more suspicious than usual, mild irritability, and difficulty sleeping. He does not meet full criteria for relapse but you are concerned this may be an early warning sign. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Immediately increase risperidone LAI to 50mg weekly
Start a course of oral risperidone 2mg PRN alongside his LAI
Arrange an urgent review, check for triggers (stress, substance use, adherence), and ensure a crisis plan is in place
Switch to clozapine as this indicates treatment resistance
distractors_rationale: Increasing the LAI dose pre-emptively is not recommended without evidence of full relapse. The patient has early warning signs that require assessment, not automatic dose escalation.
PRN oral risperidone is not indicated unless the patient is in crisis. The first step is assessment and monitoring, not automatic medication change.

CORRECT. Recognising and acting on early warning signs of relapse is a core component of relapse prevention in schizophrenia. Early warning signs are subjective or objective changes that precede full relapse by days to weeks (e.g., suspiciousness, tension, insomnia, social withdrawal, irritability). Management of early warning signs: (1) Validate the patient's experience; (2) Assess for triggers (stress, substance use, missed medication, physical illness); (3) Ensure adherence to current medication; (4) Increase contact with the community team or home treatment team; (5) Ensure a crisis/relapse prevention plan is activated; (6) Consider short-term increase in monitoring; (7) Only consider medication changes if symptoms escalate. The patient has a clear plan and early warning signs are being detected — this is the window for PREVENTION.
Hospital admission is not indicated for early warning signs without acute risk or severe symptoms. Early intervention in the community can prevent relapse and readmission.
Clozapine is for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failure of 2 adequate antipsychotic trials). This patient is stable on risperidone with early warning signs — not treatment failure.
teaching_point: Relapse prevention in schizophrenia — early warning signs: Prodromal symptoms precede full relapse by 1-6 weeks. Common early signs: tension, anxiety, insomnia, irritability, suspiciousness, social withdrawal, reduced concentration. Management: (1) Use a personalised early warning signs checklist; (2) Patient, family, and team all trained to identify them; (3) Activate a crisis/relapse prevention plan; (4) Increase contact frequency; (5) Brief low-dose antipsychotic increase (under specialist guidance); (6) Address stress and triggers. Evidence: early warning sign interventions reduce relapse rates by 20-30%. NICE CG178: 'Consider developing a relapse prevention plan with people with psychosis and schizophrenia who are in remission.' Every patient should have a WRAP (Wellness Recovery Action Plan) or personalised relapse signature plan.
source: NICE CG178; Birchwood M et al. (2000) Early warning signs in schizophrenia

stem: A 29-year-old man with a diagnosis of schizophrenia has prominent negative symptoms (avolition, anhedonia, asociality) that have been stable for 3 years. He also suffers from obesity (BMI 33) and has a history of diabetes (HbA1c 56 mmol/mol) which is well-controlled on metformin. He is currently on olanzapine 15mg daily and is intolerant of aripiprazole (akathisia). What option might improve both negative symptoms and metabolic health?
options: Increase olanzapine to 20mg to maximise D2 occupancy
Add amisulpride 100mg daily (low dose) to olanzapine
Switch to clozapine which has superior efficacy for negative symptoms
Start CBT for negative symptoms and consider switching to amisulpride
distractors_rationale: Increasing olanzapine would worsen metabolic parameters and would not improve negative symptoms (D2 occupancy >80% may worsen secondary negative symptoms via EPS).

Augmenting olanzapine with amisulpride 100mg may help negative symptoms (low-dose amisulpride enhances prefrontal dopamine) but the combination carries additive metabolic and prolactin risks. Better to switch to amisulpride monotherapy.

Clozapine has the highest metabolic risk and would worsen his metabolic health. Clozapine improves SECONDARY negative symptoms (by reducing positive symptoms and EPS) but evidence for PRIMARY negative symptoms is weaker than for amisulpride.
Fluoxetine does not have evidence for primary negative symptoms and carries CYP interactions (CYP2D6 inhibition). It may help depression if present, but this patient has no depressive symptoms.

CORRECT. CBT for negative symptoms has evidence for modest improvement in avolition, social functioning, and motivation (Grant et al., 2012; NICE CG178). Additionally, switching to amisulpride (50-300mg daily) would: (1) Improve primary negative symptoms via presynaptic D2/D3 blockade enhancing prefrontal dopamine (strongest evidence of all antipsychotics for negative symptoms); (2) Have a better metabolic profile than olanzapine (weight neutral, no diabetes risk); (3) Be suitable as monotherapy, avoiding the metabolic burden of olanzapine. Amisulpride does NOT cause weight gain or diabetes — it has the best metabolic profile of all SGAs alongside aripiprazole.
teaching_point: Amisulpride — unique among antipsychotics: At low doses (50-300mg), it preferentially blocks presynaptic D2/D3 autoreceptors, increasing dopamine release in the prefrontal cortex → improves negative symptoms. At high doses (400-800mg), it blocks postsynaptic D2/D3 receptors → treats positive symptoms. This is called the 'amisulpride double dissociation' — the only antipsychotic that is more effective at low doses for negative symptoms than at high doses. Metabolic profile: weight neutral, no diabetes risk, no dyslipidaemia. Side effects: prolactin elevation (dose-dependent), QTc prolongation at high doses. Renal excretion (avoid in renal impairment). CBT for negative symptoms: evidence for modest improvement, particularly for avolition. Key meta-analysis: Leucht et al. (2013) An J Psychiatry confirmed amisulpride's superior efficacy for negative symptoms.
source: NICE CG178; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines; Leucht S et al. (2013) Amisulpride for negative symptoms
